The simultaneous effect of chemotaxis and alarm-taxis on the global existence and stability of a predator-prey systemThanks: ∗Corresponding author

Gnanasekaran Shanmugasundaram GSDepartment of Mathematics, National Institute of Technology Tiruchirappalli, Tamilnadu 620015, India Current address: Email address: sekaran@nitt.edu , Jitraj Saha∗ JSDepartment of Mathematics, National Institute of Technology Tiruchirappalli, Tamilnadu 620015, India Current address: Email address: jitraj@nitt.edu and Rafael Díaz Fuentes RDFDepartment of Mathematics and Informatics, University of Cagliari, Via Ospedale 72, Cagliari 09124, Italy Current address: Email address: rafael.diazfuentes@unica.it
Abstract.

This study examines a fully parabolic predator–prey chemo-alarm-taxis system under homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions in a bounded domain Ω⊂ℝn\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} with a smooth boundary ∂Ω\partial\Omega. Under specific parameter conditions, it is shown that the system admits a unique, globally bounded classical solution. The convergence of the solution is established through the construction of an appropriate Lyapunov functional. In addition, numerical simulations are presented to validate the asymptotic behaviour of the solution. The results highlight the significant role of chemotaxis and alarm-taxis coefficients in determining the existence and stability of predator–prey models, as discussed in the literature.

35A01; 35A09; 35B40; 92C17; 37N25; 65N06

1. Introduction and motivation

Burglar alarm calls [3] act as a key anti-predation strategy, whereby prey emit signals that attract secondary predators, potentially deterring primary predators [5, 14]. This behaviour is observed in marine systems, such as dinoflagellates employing bioluminescence in response to copepod disturbances, which may draw fish as secondary predators [12]. Chemotaxis, on the other hand, refers to the movement of microorganisms in response to chemical gradients, with applications spanning ecology, immunology, biology and medicine.

In this context, we formulate the chemo-alarm-taxis system, in which the primary predator vv is attracted to the prey ww through a common chemical signal zz, while the prey moves away from the primary predator in response to the same chemical. At the same time, the secondary predator is drawn towards the combined density of the primary predator and the prey owing to the alarm call emitted by the prey. This interaction leads the secondary predator to prey upon the primary predator, thereby providing the prey with a potential defence mechanism against predation. To capture these ecological dynamics, we consider a system of coupled, nonlinear parabolic partial differential equations describing the interactions between two predators and one prey in a chemo-alarm-taxis framework. The system is given by

{ut=d1Δu−χ1∇⋅(u∇(vw))+μ1u(1−u+a1v+a2w),x∈Ω,t>0,vt=d2Δv−χ2∇⋅(v∇z)+μ2v(1−v−a3u+a4w),x∈Ω,t>0,wt=d3Δw+ξ∇⋅(w∇z)+μ3w(1−w−a5u−a6v),x∈Ω,t>0,zt=d4​Δ​z+α​v+β​w−γ​z,x∈Ω,t>0,∂u∂ν=∂v∂ν=∂w∂ν=∂z∂ν=0,x∈∂Ω,t>0,u⁡(x,0)=u0,v⁡(x,0)=v0,w⁡(x,0)=w0,z⁡(x,0)=z0x∈Ω,\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{llll}&u_{t}=d_{1}\Delta u-\chi_{1}\nabla\cdot\left(u\nabla(vw)\right)+\mu_{1}u(1-u+a_{1}v+a_{2}w),&x\in\Omega,\,t>0,\\ &v_{t}=d_{2}\Delta v-\chi_{2}\nabla\cdot\left(v\nabla z\right)+\mu_{2}v(1-v-a_{3}u+a_{4}w),&x\in\Omega,\,t>0,\\ &w_{t}=d_{3}\Delta w+\xi\nabla\cdot\left(w\nabla z\right)+\mu_{3}w(1-w-a_{5}u-a_{6}v),&x\in\Omega,\,t>0,\\ &z_{t}=d_{4}\Delta z+\alpha v+\beta w-\gamma z,&x\in\Omega,\,t>0,\\ &\frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}=\frac{\partial v}{\partial\nu}=\frac{\partial w}{\partial\nu}=\frac{\partial z}{\partial\nu}=0,&x\in\partial\Omega,\,t>0,\\ &u(x,0)=u_{0},\quad v(x,0)=v_{0},\quad w(x,0)=w_{0},\quad z(x,0)=z_{0\hskip 16.38895pt}&x\in\Omega,\end{array}\right.

in a bounded domain Ω⊂ℝn\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} with smooth boundary ∂Ω\partial\Omega. Here, ν\nu denotes the unit outward normal on ∂Ω\partial\Omega. The unknown functions u=u⁡(x,t)u=u(x,t) and v=v⁡(x,t)v=v(x,t) describe the population densities of the secondary predator and the primary predator, respectively. In addition, w=w⁡(x,t)w=w(x,t) represents the prey population, while z=z⁡(x,t)z=z(x,t) denotes the concentration of the chemical attractant produced by the prey. The parameters d1,d2,d3,d4,χ1,χ2,ξ,α,β,γ,μ1,μ2,μ3d_{1},d_{2},d_{3},d_{4},\chi_{1},\chi_{2},\xi,\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\mu_{1},\mu_{2},\mu_{3} and ai​(i=1,2,3,4,5,6)a_{i}\ (i=1,2,3,4,5,6) are all positive constants and the initial data u0,v0,w0,u_{0},v_{0},w_{0}, and z0z_{0} are nonnegative functions. The constants d1,d2,d3,d_{1},d_{2},d_{3}, and d4d_{4} are the diffusion coefficients, representing the natural dispersive forces governing the movement of the predators, prey and chemical concentrations, respectively. The parameter χ1\chi_{1} is the alarm-taxis coefficient, while χ2\chi_{2} and ξ\xi are the chemotactic coefficients. The term −χ1∇⋅(u∇(vw))-\chi_{1}\nabla\cdot(u\nabla(vw)) represents alarm-taxis, namely the directed movement of the secondary predator (uu) towards the gradient of the combined predator–prey density (∇(v​w)\nabla(vw)) in response to the alarm signal. Similarly, the term −χ2∇⋅(v∇z)-\chi_{2}\nabla\cdot(v\nabla z) describes chemo-attraction, that is, the directed movement of the primary predator (vv) towards the gradient of the chemical concentration (∇z\nabla z). By contrast, the term +ξ∇⋅(w∇z)+\xi\nabla\cdot(w\nabla z) denotes chemo-repulsion, meaning the directed movement of the prey (ww) away from the gradient of the chemical concentration (∇z\nabla z). The constants μ1,μ2,μ3\mu_{1},\mu_{2},\mu_{3} are the logistic growth coefficients, while a1,a2,a3,a4,a5,a6a_{1},a_{2},a_{3},a_{4},a_{5},a_{6} represent the interspecific interactions among the three species. The parameters α,β\alpha,\beta and γ\gamma correspond to the production and decay rates of the common chemical. Furthermore, we assume that the initial data u0,v0,w0,u_{0},v_{0},w_{0}, and z0z_{0} satisfy

{u0,v0,w0∈𝒞0​(Ω¯),withu0,v0,w0≥0in​Ω,z0∈𝒲1,q​(Ω¯),for some​q>n,withz0≥0in​Ω.\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{llll}&u_{0},v_{0},w_{0}\in{\mathcal{C}^{0}}(\overline{\Omega}),&\text{with}\quad u_{0},v_{0},w_{0}\geq 0\quad\text{in}\,\>\Omega,\\ &z_{0}\in{\mathcal{W}^{1,q}}(\overline{\Omega}),&\text{for some}\,\,q>n,\quad\text{with}\quad z_{0}\geq 0\quad\text{in}\,\>\Omega.\end{array}\right.

The foundational model for chemotaxis was first proposed by Keller and Segel in 1970 [13]. Since then, the Keller–Segel model and its various modifications have been extensively investigated by numerous researchers. In this context, considerable attention has been devoted to two-species–one-chemical systems [19, 22, 23, 24, 33, 35, 38] and two-species–two-chemical systems with a competing source [2, 30, 34, 37, 42]. Among these, the predator–prey model, an ecologically significant extension of the two-species competition framework, has been widely explored. Research on predator–prey systems with one-chemical chemotaxis includes [6, 20, 21], while investigations into predator–prey systems with two-chemical chemotaxis can be found in [16, 26, 27]. For further developments and extensions of predator–prey models, see [8, 28].

Motivated by the ecological significance of alarm calls, the alarm-taxis model was first introduced by Haskell and Bell [9]

{ut=η​d​ux​x+f⁡(u,v,w),vt=(d​vx−ξ​v​ux)x+g⁡(u,v,w),wt=(wx−χ​w​ϕx​(u,v))x+h⁡(u,v,w).\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{llll}&u_{t}=\eta du_{xx}+f(u,v,w),\\ &v_{t}=(dv_{x}-\xi vu_{x})_{x}+g(u,v,w),\\ &w_{t}=(w_{x}-\chi w\phi_{x}(u,v))_{x}+h(u,v,w).\end{array}\right.

Herein, u,v,u,v, and ww denote the resource or prey (e.g. dinoflagellates), the primary predator (e.g. copepods), and the secondary predator (e.g. fish), respectively. Under zero-flux boundary conditions, and for certain initial data (details of which may be omitted in subsequent discussion), the authors demonstrated the global existence of positive, bounded classical solutions in one-dimensional space. They also established the existence of non-constant equilibrium solutions and analysed their stability. In addition, numerical simulations were carried out to illustrate the emergence of spatial patterns in this model, emphasising the adaptive advantage conferred by a signalling mechanism consistent with the alarm hypothesis.

Fuest and Lankeit [7] considered the following system

{ut=d1​Δ​u+u⁡(λ1−μ1​u−a1​v−a2​w),vt=d2Δv−ξ∇⋅(v∇u)+v(λ2−μ2u+b1u−a3w),wt=d3Δw−χ∇⋅(w∇(uv))+w(λ3−μ3w+b2u+b3v),\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{llll}&u_{t}=d_{1}\Delta u+u(\lambda_{1}-\mu_{1}u-a_{1}v-a_{2}w),\\ &v_{t}=d_{2}\Delta v-\xi\nabla\cdot\left(v\nabla u\right)+v(\lambda_{2}-\mu_{2}u+b_{1}u-a_{3}w),\\ &w_{t}=d_{3}\Delta w-\chi\nabla\cdot\left(w\nabla(uv)\right)+w(\lambda_{3}-\mu_{3}w+b_{2}u+b_{3}v),\end{array}\right.

with homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions, the system models the interactions among the prey uu, the predator vv, and the superpredator ww, the latter preying on both of the other populations. The authors established the existence of a global classical solution in the case of pure alarm-taxis, i.e. when ξ=0\xi=0. For ξ>0\xi>0, they investigated the existence of global generalised solutions.

Li and Wang [17] considered the following system

{ut=d1​Δ​u+r1​u​(1−u)−b1​u​v−b3​u​w,vt=d2Δv−ξ∇⋅(v∇u)+r2v(1−v)+uv−b2vw,wt=d3Δw−χ∇⋅(w∇(uv))+r3w(1−wσ)+vw+uw,\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{llll}&u_{t}=d_{1}\Delta u+r_{1}u(1-u)-b_{1}uv-b_{3}uw,\\ &v_{t}=d_{2}\Delta v-\xi\nabla\cdot\left(v\nabla u\right)+r_{2}v(1-v)+uv-b_{2}vw,\\ &w_{t}=d_{3}\Delta w-\chi\nabla\cdot\left(w\nabla(uv)\right)+r_{3}w(1-w^{\sigma})+vw+uw,\end{array}\right.

where u,v,u,v, and ww denote the densities of the prey, the primary predator, and the secondary predator, respectively. By applying semi-group theory, the authors established the boundedness of classical solutions in two spatial dimensions. They replaced the usual logistic term r3​w​(1−w)r_{3}w(1-w) with r3​w​(1−wσ)r_{3}w(1-w^{\sigma}) in order to investigate how large the intra-species competition exponent must be to guarantee the global boundedness of solutions. Furthermore, asymptotic stability was obtained through the construction of a suitable Lyapunov functional.

Jin et al. [12] studied the global existence of classical solutions to the following system by employing the Neumann heat semigroup technique in two spatial dimensions

{ut=d1​Δ​u+μ1​u​(1−u)−b1​u​v−b3​u​wu+w,vt=d2Δv−ξ∇⋅(v∇u)+μ2v(1−v)+uv−b2vw,wt=d3Δw−χ∇⋅(w∇(uv))+μ3w(1−w)+vw+c3u​wu+w.\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{llll}&u_{t}=d_{1}\Delta u+\mu_{1}u(1-u)-b_{1}uv-b_{3}\frac{uw}{u+w},\\ &v_{t}=d_{2}\Delta v-\xi\nabla\cdot\left(v\nabla u\right)+\mu_{2}v(1-v)+uv-b_{2}vw,\\ &w_{t}=d_{3}\Delta w-\chi\nabla\cdot\left(w\nabla(uv)\right)+\mu_{3}w(1-w)+vw+c_{3}\frac{uw}{u+w}.\end{array}\right.

Additionally, the authors established the global asymptotic stability for the cases where b3=c3=0b_{3}=c_{3}=0 and b3>0,c3>0b_{3}>0,c_{3}>0.

Zhang et al. [40] studied the following food chain model incorporating alarm-taxis and logistic growth

{ut=d1​Δ​u+u⁡(1−u)−b1​u​v,vt=d2Δv−ξ∇⋅(v∇u)+θ1v(1−v)+uv−b2vw,wt=d3Δw−χ∇⋅(w∇(uv))+θ2w(1−w)+vw.\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{llll}&u_{t}=d_{1}\Delta u+u(1-u)-b_{1}uv,\\ &v_{t}=d_{2}\Delta v-\xi\nabla\cdot\left(v\nabla u\right)+\theta_{1}v(1-v)+uv-b_{2}vw,\\ &w_{t}=d_{3}\Delta w-\chi\nabla\cdot\left(w\nabla(uv)\right)+\theta_{2}w(1-w)+vw.\end{array}\right.

The authors showed that, for sufficiently large values of θ1\theta_{1} and θ2\theta_{2}, the system admits a globally bounded classical solution when n≥3n\geq 3. Moreover, by constructing an appropriate Lyapunov functional, they demonstrated that, under certain parameter conditions, the system converges either to a coexistence state or to a semi-coexistence state as t→∞t\to\infty.

Zhang and Chen [39] studied the global existence of the following system

{ut=d1​Δ​u+u⁡(1−u−a​vv+ρ),vt=d2​Δ​v+v⁡(b​uv+ρ−α−c​ww+σ),wt=d3Δw−χ∇⋅(w∇(uv))+w(m​vw+σ−β),\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{llll}&u_{t}=d_{1}\Delta u+u\left(1-u-\frac{av}{v+\rho}\right),\\ &v_{t}=d_{2}\Delta v+v\left(\frac{bu}{v+\rho}-\alpha-\frac{cw}{w+\sigma}\right),\\ &w_{t}=d_{3}\Delta w-\chi\nabla\cdot\left(w\nabla(uv)\right)+w\left(\frac{mv}{w+\sigma}-\beta\right),\end{array}\right.

for n≥1n\geq 1 with sufficiently smooth initial data. The authors analysed the large-time behaviour of the system under certain conditions and derived convergence rates. In addition, numerical simulations were carried out to validate the analytical results.

To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to rigorously establish the global existence, boundedness, and convergence of solutions in a predator–prey system incorporating both chemotaxis and alarm-taxis. Motivated by the existing literature, our primary objective is to demonstrate the existence of a global classical solution to system (1), which remains uniformly bounded in Ω×(0,∞)\Omega\times(0,\infty) for n≥1n\geq 1. Furthermore, we establish convergence of the solution by constructing a suitable Lyapunov functional. Finally, we perform numerical simulations to confirm the asymptotic behaviour of solutions in both two and three spatial dimensions.

The remainder of this article is organised as follows. Section 2 introduces preliminary lemmas and establishes the local existence of the classical solution. Section 3 is devoted to proving the global existence and boundedness of classical solutions for system (1). In Section 4, we carry out a stability analysis, while Section 5 presents numerical validation and results. The paper concludes with a summary in Section 6. Our main result on global existence is the following.

Theorem 1.1 (Global existence of solutions).

Suppose that Ω⊂ℝn​(n≥1)\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}(n\geq 1), is a bounded domain with smooth boundary. Then there exists μ>0\mu>0, such that if min⁡{μ2,μ3}>μ\min\{\mu_{2},\mu_{3}\}>\mu and for any nonnegative initial data (u0,v0,w0,z0)(u_{0},v_{0},w_{0},z_{0}) satisfying (1) for some q>max⁡{2,n}q>\max\{2,n\}, the system (1) possesses a unique classical solution (u,v,w,z)(u,v,w,z) which is uniformly bounded in the sense that

‖u⁡(⋅,t)‖ℒ∞​(Ω)+‖v⁡(⋅,t)‖𝒲1,∞​(Ω)+‖w⁡(⋅,t)‖𝒲1,∞​(Ω)+‖z⁡(⋅,t)‖𝒲1,q​(Ω)≤C,∀t>0,\displaystyle\big\|u(\cdot,t)\big\|_{{\mathcal{L}^{\infty}}(\Omega)}+\big\|v(\cdot,t)\big\|_{{\mathcal{W}^{1,\infty}}(\Omega)}+\big\|w(\cdot,t)\big\|_{{\mathcal{W}^{1,\infty}}(\Omega)}+\big\|z(\cdot,t)\big\|_{{\mathcal{W}^{1,q}}(\Omega)}\leq C,\quad\forall\,t>0,

where the constant C>0C>0.

Remark 1.1.

In the one-dimensional case n=1n=1, global existence can be established under weaker conditions. This follows directly from the testing procedures and regularity results presented in Section 3.

Now, we examine the equilibrium points of the system. Let (u,v,w,z)(u,v,w,z) be a classical solution of (1) satisfying (1) and (ue,ve,we,ze)(u_{e},v_{e},w_{e},z_{e}) denote the equilibrium points of the system (1), satisfying the following system of equations

{μ1​ue​(1−ue+a1​ve+a2​we)=0,μ2​ve​(1−ve−a3​ue+a4​we)=0,μ3​we​(1−we−a5​ue−a6​ve)=0,α​ve+β​we−γ​ze=0.\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{rrll}\mu_{1}u_{e}(1-u_{e}+a_{1}v_{e}+a_{2}w_{e})=&0,\\ \mu_{2}v_{e}(1-v_{e}-a_{3}u_{e}+a_{4}w_{e})=&0,\\ \mu_{3}w_{e}(1-w_{e}-a_{5}u_{e}-a_{6}v_{e})=&0,\\ \alpha v_{e}+\beta w_{e}-\gamma z_{e}=&0.\end{array}\right.

    ​(1+a11+a1​a3,1−a31+a1​a3,0,α⁡(1−a3)γ⁡(1+a1​a3))    \displaystyle{\left(0,\frac{1+a_{4}}{1+a_{4}a_{6}},\frac{1-a_{6}}{1+a_{4}a_{6}},\frac{\alpha(1+a_{4})+\beta(1-a_{6})}{\gamma(1+a_{4}a_{6})}\right),\left(\frac{1+a_{2}}{1+a_{2}a_{5}},0,\frac{1-a_{5}}{1+a_{2}a_{5}},\frac{\beta(1-a_{5})}{\gamma(1+a_{2}a_{5})}\right)},\quad\text{and}\\ \displaystyle{\left(\frac{1+a_{1}}{1+a_{1}a_{3}},\frac{1-a_{3}}{1+a_{1}a_{3}},0,\frac{\alpha(1-a_{3})}{\gamma(1+a_{1}a_{3})}\right)}    .

Here, (0,0,0,0) represents the extinction equilibrium where all species vanish; (1,0,0,0) corresponds to the equilibrium with only the secondary predator present; (0,1,0,αγ)\left(0,1,0,\frac{\alpha}{\gamma}\right) describes the primary predator-only equilibrium and (0,0,1,βγ)\left(0,0,1,\frac{\beta}{\gamma}\right) characterizes the prey-only equilibrium. Additionally, there exist three semi-coexistence equilibria where any two species persist together. The most ecologically significant state, (u∗,v∗,w∗,z∗)(u^{*},v^{*},w^{*},z^{*}), represents the coexistence equilibrium where all three species maintain stable populations. Here, the coexistence steady state (u∗,v∗,w∗,z∗)(u^{*},v^{*},w^{*},z^{*}) is explicitly given by

Among the eight possible equilibrium points, we analyze four biologically relevant cases: (i) the coexistence steady state (ii) the trivial steady state (1, 0, 0, 0) (iii) two semi-coexistence steady states. Using a suitable Lyapunov functional, we establish the asymptotic stability. Theorem 1.2 (Coexistence state of the species).

2. Preliminaries and local existence

The aim of this section is to concentrate on the basic estimates and the local existence of the classical solution. The local existence lemma is constructed based on ideas derived from Horstmann [11] and Tello [32], along with the references cited therein.

From now on, all the constants Ci,i=1,2,…C_{i},i=1,2,\ldots, are assumed to be positive and the numbering is restarted for each proof.

+∫s0te−γ⁡(t−s)∥∇ed4​(t−s)​Δ(αv(⋅,s)+βw(⋅,s))∥ℒr​l​(Ω)ds.\displaystyle+\int^{t}_{s_{0}}e^{-\gamma(t-s)}\Big\|\nabla e^{d_{4}(t-s)\Delta}\Big(\alpha v(\cdot,s)+\beta w(\cdot,s)\Big)\Big\|_{{\mathcal{L}^{rl}}(\Omega)}\mathrm{d}s.

+C2∫s0te−γ⁡(t−s)(1+(t−s)−12−n2​(1p−1r​l))e−λ​d4​(t−s)∥αv(⋅,s)+βw(⋅,s)∥ℒp​(Ω)ds,\displaystyle+C_{2}\int^{t}_{s_{0}}e^{-\gamma(t-s)}\Big(1+(t-s)^{-\frac{1}{2}-\frac{n}{2}(\frac{1}{p}-\frac{1}{rl})}\Big)e^{-\lambda d_{4}(t-s)}\big\|\alpha v(\cdot,s)+\beta w(\cdot,s)\big\|_{{\mathcal{L}^{p}}(\Omega)}\mathrm{d}s,

Lemma 3.3.

Suppose that the assumptions in Lemma 3.2 hold true. There exists K5>0K_{5}>0 fulfilling

∫tt+τ∫Ω|Δ​z​(⋅,t)|2≤K5,\displaystyle\int_{t}^{t+\tau}\int_{\Omega}\big|\Delta z(\cdot,t)\big|^{2}\leq K_{5},

for all t∈(0,Tmax−τ)t\in(0,T_{\mathrm{max}}-\tau).

Proof.

Multiplying the fourth equation in (1) with −2​Δ​z-2\Delta z and integrating by parts, we obtain

dd​t​∫Ω|∇z|2≤\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\int_{\Omega}|{\nabla z}|^{2}\leq −2d4∫Ω|Δz|2+2α∥v∥ℒ∞​(Ω)∫ΩΔz+2β∥w∥ℒ∞​(Ω)∫ΩΔz−2γ∫Ω|∇z|2.\displaystyle-2d_{4}\int_{\Omega}|\Delta z|^{2}+2\alpha\big\|v\big\|_{{\mathcal{L}^{\infty}}(\Omega)}\int_{\Omega}\Delta z+2\beta\big\|w\big\|_{{\mathcal{L}^{\infty}}(\Omega)}\int_{\Omega}\Delta z-2\gamma\int_{\Omega}|{\nabla z}|^{2}.

Simplifying one gets

dd​t​∫Ω|∇z|2+2​γ​∫Ω|∇z|2+2​d4​∫Ω|Δ​z|2≤2​α​K4​∫ΩΔ​z+2​β​K4​∫ΩΔ​z≤d4​∫Ω|Δ​z|2+C1.\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\int_{\Omega}|{\nabla z}|^{2}+2\gamma\int_{\Omega}|{\nabla z}|^{2}+2d_{4}\int_{\Omega}|\Delta z|^{2}\leq 2\alpha K_{4}\int_{\Omega}\Delta z+2\beta K_{4}\int_{\Omega}\Delta z\leq d_{4}\int_{\Omega}|\Delta z|^{2}+C_{1}.

Finally,

dd​t​∫Ω|∇z|2+2​γ​∫Ω|∇z|2+d4​∫Ω|Δ​z|2≤C1,∀t∈(0,Tmax),\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\int_{\Omega}|{\nabla z}|^{2}+2\gamma\int_{\Omega}|{\nabla z}|^{2}+d_{4}\int_{\Omega}|\Delta z|^{2}\leq C_{1},\qquad\forall\,t\in(0,T_{\mathrm{max}}), (3.26)

where C1>0C_{1}>0. Now, integrate (3.26) over (t,t+τ)(t,t+\tau) to get

∫tt+τ∫Ω|Δ​z​(⋅,t)|2≤C2,∀t∈(0,Tmax−τ),\displaystyle\int_{t}^{t+\tau}\int_{\Omega}\big|\Delta z(\cdot,t)\big|^{2}\leq C_{2},\qquad\forall\,t\in(0,T_{\mathrm{max}}-\tau),

where C2>0C_{2}>0. This completes the proof. ∎

Lemma 3.4.

Suppose that Ω⊂ℝn​(n≥1)\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}(n\geq 1), is a bounded domain with smooth boundary and the assumptions in Lemma 3.2 hold true. There exists K6>0K_{6}>0 fulfilling

∫Ω|∇v​(⋅,t)|2≤K6,\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}|\nabla v(\cdot,t)|^{2}\leq K_{6}, (3.27)

for all t∈(0,Tmax)t\in(0,T_{\mathrm{max}}).

Proof.

Multiplying the second equation in (1) with −2​Δ​v-2\Delta v and integrating by parts, we obtain

dd​t​∫Ω|∇v|2=\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\int_{\Omega}|{\nabla v}|^{2}= −2d2∫Ω|Δv|2+2χ2∫Ω∇v⋅∇zΔv+2χ2∫ΩvΔzΔv+2μ2∫Ω|∇v|2\displaystyle-2d_{2}\int_{\Omega}|\Delta v|^{2}+2\chi_{2}\int_{\Omega}\nabla v\cdot{\nabla z}\Delta v+2\chi_{2}\int_{\Omega}v\Delta z\Delta v+2\mu_{2}\int_{\Omega}|{\nabla v}|^{2}
−2μ2∫Ω∇v2⋅∇v+2μ2a3∫ΩuvΔv−2μ2a4∫ΩvwΔv\displaystyle-2\mu_{2}\int_{\Omega}{\nabla v}^{2}\cdot{\nabla v}+2\mu_{2}a_{3}\int_{\Omega}uv\Delta v-2\mu_{2}a_{4}\int_{\Omega}vw\Delta v
≤\displaystyle\leq −2d2∫Ω|Δv|2+2χ2∫Ω∇v⋅∇zΔv+2χ2∫ΩvΔzΔv+2μ2∫Ω|∇v|2−4μ2∫Ωv|∇v|2\displaystyle-2d_{2}\int_{\Omega}|\Delta v|^{2}+2\chi_{2}\int_{\Omega}\nabla v\cdot{\nabla z}{{\Delta v}}+2\chi_{2}\int_{\Omega}v{{\Delta z}}\Delta v+2\mu_{2}\int_{\Omega}|{\nabla v}|^{2}-4\mu_{2}\int_{\Omega}v|{\nabla v}|^{2}
+2μ2a3∫ΩuvΔv−2μ2a4∫ΩvwΔv.\displaystyle+2\mu_{2}a_{3}\int_{\Omega}uv\Delta v-2\mu_{2}a_{4}\int_{\Omega}vw\Delta v.

Rearranging the terms, we get

dd​t​∫Ω|∇v|2+2​μ2​∫Ω|∇v|2+2​d2​∫Ω|Δ​v|2≤\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\int_{\Omega}|{\nabla v}|^{2}+2\mu_{2}\int_{\Omega}|{\nabla v}|^{2}+2d_{2}\int_{\Omega}|\Delta v|^{2}\leq  2χ2∫Ω∇v⋅∇zΔv+2χ2∥v∥ℒ∞​(Ω)∫Ω|Δz||Δv|\displaystyle\>2\chi_{2}\int_{\Omega}\nabla v\cdot{\nabla z}\>\Delta v+2\chi_{2}\big\|v\big\|_{{\mathcal{L}^{\infty}}(\Omega)}\int_{\Omega}|\Delta z||\Delta v|
+4μ2∫Ω|∇v|2+2μ2a3∥v∥ℒ∞​(Ω)∫Ωu|Δv|\displaystyle+4\mu_{2}\int_{\Omega}|{\nabla v}|^{2}+2\mu_{2}a_{3}\big\|v\big\|_{{\mathcal{L}^{\infty}}(\Omega)}\int_{\Omega}u|\Delta v|
+2​μ2​a4​‖v‖ℒ∞​(Ω)|w|∫Ωℒ∞​(Ω)⁡|Δ​v|.\displaystyle+2\mu_{2}a_{4}\big\|v\big\|_{{\mathcal{L}^{\infty}}(\Omega)}\big\|w\big\|_{{\mathcal{L}^{\infty}}(\Omega)}\int_{\Omega}|\Delta v|.\ (3.28)

The Hölder inequality gives for the first term in RHS of (3.28),

2χ2∫Ω∇v⋅∇zΔv≤2χ2∥∇v∥ℒ4​(Ω)∥∇z∥ℒ4​(Ω)∥Δv∥ℒ2​(Ω).\displaystyle 2\chi_{2}\int_{\Omega}\nabla v\cdot{\nabla z}\>\Delta v\leq 2\chi_{2}\big\|{\nabla v}\big\|_{{\mathcal{L}^{4}}(\Omega)}\|{\nabla z}\|_{{\mathcal{L}^{4}}(\Omega)}\big\|\Delta v\big\|_{{\mathcal{L}^{2}}(\Omega)}. (3.29)

The Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality with Lemma 3.2 gives

2​χ2​‖∇v‖ℒ4​(Ω)≤\displaystyle 2\chi_{2}\big\|{\nabla v}\big\|_{{\mathcal{L}^{4}}(\Omega)}\leq C1​‖Δ​v‖ℒ2​(Ω)12​‖v‖ℒ∞​(Ω)12≤C2​‖Δ​v‖ℒ2​(Ω)12,\displaystyle C_{1}\big\|\Delta v\big\|^{\frac{1}{2}}_{{\mathcal{L}^{2}}(\Omega)}\big\|v\big\|^{\frac{1}{2}}_{{\mathcal{L}^{\infty}}(\Omega)}\leq C_{2}\big\|\Delta v\big\|^{\frac{1}{2}}_{{\mathcal{L}^{2}}(\Omega)}, (3.30)

where C1,C2>0C_{1},C_{2}>0. Substituting the estimate (3.30) into (3.29) and using the boundedness of ‖∇z‖ℒ4​(Ω)\|{\nabla z}\|_{{\mathcal{L}^{4}}(\Omega)} from (3.17), which holds due to the condition r​l≥4rl\geq 4, we then apply Young inequality to obtain

2χ2∫Ω∇v⋅∇zΔv≤\displaystyle 2\chi_{2}\int_{\Omega}{\nabla v}\cdot{\nabla z}\Delta v\leq C2​‖Δ​v‖ℒ2​(Ω)32​‖∇z‖ℒ4​(Ω)≤2​d25​‖Δ​v‖ℒ2​(Ω)2+C3,\displaystyle C_{2}\big\|\Delta v\big\|_{{\mathcal{L}^{2}}(\Omega)}^{\frac{3}{2}}\|{\nabla z}\|_{{\mathcal{L}^{4}}(\Omega)}\leq\frac{2d_{2}}{5}\big\|\Delta v\big\|^{2}_{{\mathcal{L}^{2}}(\Omega)}+C_{3}, (3.31)

where C3>0C_{3}>0. Now using the Young inequality for the second term in RHS of (3.28), to get

2​χ2​K4​∫Ω|Δ​v|​|Δ​z|≤2​d25​‖Δ​v‖ℒ2​(Ω)2+C4​‖Δ​z‖ℒ2​(Ω)2,\displaystyle 2\chi_{2}K_{4}\int_{\Omega}|\Delta v||\Delta z|\leq\frac{2d_{2}}{5}\big\|\Delta v\big\|^{2}_{{\mathcal{L}^{2}}(\Omega)}+C_{4}\big\|\Delta z\big\|^{2}_{{\mathcal{L}^{2}}(\Omega)}, (3.32)

where C4>0C_{4}>0. Using the Hölder inequality and the Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality for the third term in RHS of (3.28) with C5>0C_{5}>0, gives

4​μ2​∫Ω|∇v|2≤4​μ2​(∫Ω|∇v|4)12​|Ω|12≤4​μ2​|Ω|12​‖∇v‖ℒ4​(Ω)2≤\displaystyle 4\mu_{2}\int_{\Omega}|{\nabla v}|^{2}\leq{4\mu_{2}}\left(\int_{\Omega}|{\nabla v}|^{4}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}|\Omega|^{\frac{1}{2}}\leq{4\mu_{2}}|\Omega|^{\frac{1}{2}}\big\|{\nabla v}\big\|^{2}_{{\mathcal{L}^{4}}(\Omega)}\leq 2​d25​‖Δ​v‖ℒ2​(Ω)2+C5.\displaystyle\frac{2d_{2}}{5}\big\|\Delta v\big\|^{2}_{{\mathcal{L}^{2}}(\Omega)}+C_{5}. (3.33)

Once again Cauchy’s inequality for the last two terms in (3.28), gives

2​μ2​a3​K4​∫Ωu​|Δ​v|≤2​d25​‖Δ​v‖ℒ2​(Ω)2+C6​‖u‖ℒ2​(Ω)2\displaystyle 2\mu_{2}a_{3}K_{4}\int_{\Omega}u|\Delta v|\leq\frac{2d_{2}}{5}\big\|\Delta v\big\|^{2}_{{\mathcal{L}^{2}}(\Omega)}+C_{6}\big\|u\big\|^{2}_{{\mathcal{L}^{2}}(\Omega)} (3.34)

and

where C6,C7>0C_{6},C_{7}>0. Substituting (3.31)-(3.35) in to (3.28) with C8>0C_{8}>0, one gets

∫Ω|∇v|2≤C9,∀t∈(0,Tmax),\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}|{\nabla v}|^{2}\leq C_{9},\qquad\forall\,t\in(0,T_{\mathrm{max}}),

Lemma 3.5.

Proof.

Multiplying the third equation in (1) with −2​Δ​w-2\Delta w and integrating by parts, we obtain

dd​t​∫Ω|∇w|2+2​μ3​∫Ω|∇w|2+2​d2​∫Ω|Δ​w|2≤ 2ξ∫Ω∇w⋅∇zΔw+2ξ∥w∥ℒ∞​(Ω)∫Ω|Δz||Δw|+4μ3∫Ω|∇w|2−4μ3∫Ωw|∇w|2+2​μ3​a4|w|∫Ωℒ∞​(Ω)⁡u​|Δ​w|+2​μ3​a5​‖v‖ℒ∞​(Ω)|w|∫Ωℒ∞​(Ω)⁡|Δ​w|.\begin{split}\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\int_{\Omega}|{\nabla w}|^{2}+2\mu_{3}\int_{\Omega}|{\nabla w}|^{2}+2d_{2}\int_{\Omega}|\Delta w|^{2}\leq&\>2\xi\int_{\Omega}{\nabla w}\cdot{\nabla z}\Delta w+2\xi\big\|w\big\|_{{\mathcal{L}^{\infty}}(\Omega)}\int_{\Omega}|\Delta z||\Delta w|\\ &+4\mu_{3}\int_{\Omega}|{\nabla w}|^{2}-4\mu_{3}\int_{\Omega}w|{\nabla w}|^{2}\\ &+2\mu_{3}a_{4}\big\|w\big\|_{{\mathcal{L}^{\infty}}(\Omega)}\int_{\Omega}u|\Delta w|\\ &+2\mu_{3}a_{5}\big\|v\big\|_{{\mathcal{L}^{\infty}}(\Omega)}\big\|w\big\|_{{\mathcal{L}^{\infty}}(\Omega)}\int_{\Omega}|\Delta w|.\end{split} (3.37)

(3.38)

Applying the Young inequality for the second term of (3.37) gives

Using the Hölder inequality and the Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality to the third from of (3.37), gives

where C4>0C_{4}>0. The Cauchy inequality gives

+C8∫s0t(1+(t−s)−12−n2​l)ll−1e−λ​d3​ll−1​(t−s)ds+C9∫s0t∥Δz∥ℒl​(Ω)l\displaystyle+C_{8}\int^{t}_{s_{0}}\Big(1+(t-s)^{-\frac{1}{2}-\frac{n}{2l}}\Big)^{\frac{l}{l-1}}e^{-\frac{\lambda d_{3}l}{l-1}(t-s)}\mathrm{d}s+C_{9}\int^{t}_{s_{0}}\big\|\Delta z\big\|_{{\mathcal{L}^{l}}(\Omega)}^{l} (3.47)
+C10∫s0t(1+(t−s)−12−n2​l)e−λ​d3​(t−s)ds.\displaystyle+C_{10}\int^{t}_{s_{0}}\Big(1+(t-s)^{-\frac{1}{2}-\frac{n}{2l}}\Big)e^{-\lambda d_{3}(t-s)}\mathrm{d}s.

There exits Cl>0C_{l}>0, the maximal Sobolev regularity for ‖Δ​z‖ℒl​(Ω)l\big\|\Delta z\big\|_{{\mathcal{L}^{l}}(\Omega)}^{l} (l>nl>n) along with Lemma 3.1 gives

≤\displaystyle\leq C11​∫s0t‖v‖ℒl​(Ω)l+C12​∫s0t‖w‖ℒl​(Ω)l+C13\displaystyle C_{11}\int^{t}_{s_{0}}\big\|v\big\|_{{\mathcal{L}^{l}}(\Omega)}^{l}+C_{12}\int^{t}_{s_{0}}\big\|w\big\|_{{\mathcal{L}^{l}}(\Omega)}^{l}+C_{13}
≤\displaystyle\leq C14∀t∈(s0,Tmax).\displaystyle C_{14}\qquad\forall t\in(s_{0},T_{\mathrm{max}}).

where C14>0C_{14}>0. Now using the Gamma function with C15,C16>0C_{15},C_{16}>0, one gets from (3.47)

where C19>0C_{19}>0. Now, applying the variation of constants formula to the first equation of (1), we get

By Lemma 3.2 and 3.6, the bounds on the solution components hold for all t∈(0,Tmax)t\in(0,T_{\mathrm{max}}), which contradicts the blow-up criterion in (2.1). 4. Global asymptotic stability

In this section, we analyze the global asymptotic behaviour of solutions for the system (1), using the Lyapunov functional. The proofs of these asymptotic results are based on the work presented in [1]. The proof of the following lemma is adapted from [12].

Lemma 4.1.

Let (u,v,w,z)(u,v,w,z) be the nonnegative classical solution of the system (1) and suppose that the assumptions of Theorem 1.1 hold true. Then there exists θ∈(0,1)\theta\in(0,1) and C>0C>0 such that

‖u⁡(⋅,t)‖𝒞2+θ,1+θ2​(Ω¯×[t,t+1])+‖v⁡(⋅,t)‖𝒞2+θ,1+θ2​(Ω¯×[t,t+1])≤C\displaystyle\Big\|u(\cdot,t)\Big\|_{\mathcal{C}^{2+\theta,1+\frac{\theta}{2}}(\overline{\Omega}\times[t,t+1])}+\Big\|v(\cdot,t)\Big\|_{\mathcal{C}^{2+\theta,1+\frac{\theta}{2}}(\overline{\Omega}\times[t,t+1])}\leq C

and

‖w⁡(⋅,t)‖𝒞2+θ,1+θ2​(Ω¯×[t,t+1])+‖z⁡(⋅,t)‖𝒞2+θ,1+θ2​(Ω¯×[t,t+1])≤C,\displaystyle\Big\|w(\cdot,t)\Big\|_{\mathcal{C}^{2+\theta,1+\frac{\theta}{2}}(\overline{\Omega}\times[t,t+1])}+\Big\|z(\cdot,t)\Big\|_{\mathcal{C}^{2+\theta,1+\frac{\theta}{2}}(\overline{\Omega}\times[t,t+1])}\leq C,

for all t≥1t\geq 1.

Proof.

The proof is based on the standard parabolic regularity theory in [15] and Lemma 3.2 and 3.6. For more details see [18, 25]. ∎

By Lemma 4.1, it is clear that u,v,w,zu,v,w,z are continuous and bounded in Ω¯×[t,t+1]\overline{\Omega}\times[t,t+1] and the first derivatives ∇u,∇v,∇w,∇z\nabla u,\nabla v,\nabla w,\nabla z exist and are Hölder continuous. Since the Hölder norms are uniformly bounded, the gradients are also uniformly bounded in ℒ∞​(Ω){\mathcal{L}^{\infty}}(\Omega), we conclude that

‖u⁡(⋅,t)‖𝒲1,∞​(Ω),‖v⁡(⋅,t)‖𝒲1,∞​(Ω),‖w⁡(⋅,t)‖𝒲1,∞​(Ω),‖z⁡(⋅,t)‖𝒲1,∞​(Ω)≤C,\displaystyle\big\|u(\cdot,t)\big\|_{{\mathcal{W}^{1,\infty}}(\Omega)},\big\|v(\cdot,t)\big\|_{{\mathcal{W}^{1,\infty}}(\Omega)},\big\|w(\cdot,t)\big\|_{{\mathcal{W}^{1,\infty}}(\Omega)},\big\|z(\cdot,t)\big\|_{{\mathcal{W}^{1,\infty}}(\Omega)}\leq C, (4.1)

where CC is a constant independent of tt.

for t>0t>0, where

In view of Lemma 4.3, the proof is similar. ∎

4.4. Proof of the main theorems

Proof of Theorem 1.2. Let ℋ⁡(u)=u−ue​ln⁡u\mathcal{H}(u)=u-u_{e}\ln u, for u>0u>0. By applying L’Hôpital’s rule, we obtain

limu→ueℋ⁡(u)−ℋ⁡(ue)(u−ue)2=1−ueu2​(u−ue)=12​ue.\displaystyle\lim\limits_{u\to u_{e}}\frac{\mathcal{H}(u)-\mathcal{H}(u_{e})}{(u-u_{e})^{2}}=\frac{1-\frac{u_{e}}{u}}{2(u-u_{e})}=\frac{1}{2u_{e}}.

We can therefore select t0>0t_{0}>0 and use the Taylor expansion to obtain

∫Ω(u−ue−ue​ln⁡uue)=∫Ω(ℋ⁡(u)−ℋ⁡(ue))≤12​ue​∫Ω(u−ue)2,∀t>t0.\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}\left(u-u_{e}-u_{e}\ln\frac{u}{u_{e}}\right)=\int_{\Omega}(\mathcal{H}(u)-\mathcal{H}(u_{e}))\leq\frac{1}{2u_{e}}\int_{\Omega}(u-u_{e})^{2},\quad\forall\,t>t_{0}.

From the above estimate, we arrive at

14​ue​∫Ω(u−ue)2≤∫Ω(u−ue−ue​ln⁡uue)≤34​ue​∫Ω(u−ue)2,∀t>t0.\displaystyle\frac{1}{4u_{e}}\int_{\Omega}(u-u_{e})^{2}\leq\int_{\Omega}\left(u-u_{e}-u_{e}\ln\frac{u}{u_{e}}\right)\leq\frac{3}{4u_{e}}\int_{\Omega}(u-u_{e})^{2},\quad\forall\,t>t_{0}. (4.37)

Similarly, we obtain

14​ve​∫Ω(v−ve)2≤∫Ω(v−ve−ve​ln⁡vve)≤34​ve​∫Ω(v−ve)2,∀t>t0\displaystyle\frac{1}{4v_{e}}\int_{\Omega}(v-v_{e})^{2}\leq\int_{\Omega}\left(v-v_{e}-v_{e}\ln\frac{v}{v_{e}}\right)\leq\frac{3}{4v_{e}}\int_{\Omega}(v-v_{e})^{2},\quad\forall\,t>t_{0} (4.38)

and

14​we​∫Ω(w−we)2≤∫Ω(w−we−we​ln⁡wwe)≤34​we​∫Ω(w−we)2,∀t>t0.\displaystyle\frac{1}{4w_{e}}\int_{\Omega}(w-w_{e})^{2}\leq\int_{\Omega}\left(w-w_{e}-w_{e}\ln\frac{w}{w_{e}}\right)\leq\frac{3}{4w_{e}}\int_{\Omega}(w-w_{e})^{2},\quad\forall\,t>t_{0}. (4.39)

Taking into account the inequalities (4.37)-(4.39), it is clear that for all t>t0t>t_{0} and with κ1,κ2>0\kappa_{1},\kappa_{2}>0, we have

κ1​f1​(t)≤ℰ1​(t)≤κ2​f1​(t).\displaystyle\kappa_{1}f_{1}(t)\leq\mathcal{E}_{1}(t)\leq\kappa_{2}f_{1}(t). (4.40)

From (4.9) and right-hand side of (4.40), we get

dd​t​ℰ1​(t)≤−σ1​f1​(t)≤−σ1κ2​ℰ1​(t),t>t0.\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\mathcal{E}_{1}(t)\leq-\sigma_{1}f_{1}(t)\leq-\frac{\sigma_{1}}{\kappa_{2}}\mathcal{E}_{1}(t),\qquad t>t_{0}.

Solving the above differential inequality gives

ℰ1​(t)≤C1​e−σ1κ2​t,t>t0,\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{1}(t)\leq C_{1}e^{-\frac{\sigma_{1}}{\kappa_{2}}t},\qquad t>t_{0},

where C1>0C_{1}>0. Now, the left-hand side of (4.40) gives

f1​(t)≤1κ1​ℰ1​(t)≤C1κ1​e−σ1κ2​t,t>t0.\displaystyle f_{1}(t)\leq\frac{1}{\kappa_{1}}\mathscr{E}_{1}(t)\leq\frac{C_{1}}{\kappa_{1}}e^{-\frac{\sigma_{1}}{\kappa_{2}}t},\qquad t>t_{0}.

In view of (4.10) and then Lemma 4.1, finally we arrive at

‖u⁡(⋅,t)−ue‖ℒ∞​(Ω)+‖v⁡(⋅,t)−ve‖ℒ∞​(Ω)+‖w⁡(⋅,t)−we‖ℒ∞​(Ω)+‖z⁡(⋅,t)−ze‖ℒ∞​(Ω)≤C2​e−σ1κ2​t,\displaystyle\big\|u(\cdot,t)-u_{e}\big\|_{{\mathcal{L}^{\infty}}(\Omega)}+\big\|v(\cdot,t)-v_{e}\big\|_{{\mathcal{L}^{\infty}}(\Omega)}+\big\|w(\cdot,t)-w_{e}\big\|_{{\mathcal{L}^{\infty}}(\Omega)}+\big\|z(\cdot,t)-z_{e}\big\|_{{\mathcal{L}^{\infty}}(\Omega)}\leq C_{2}e^{-\frac{\sigma_{1}}{\kappa_{2}}t},

for all t>t0t>t_{0}, with C2>0C_{2}>0. This completes the proof. ∎

14​∫Ω(u−1)2≤∫Ω(u−1−ln⁡u)≤34​∫Ω(u−1)2,\displaystyle\frac{1}{4}\int_{\Omega}\left(u-1\right)^{2}\leq\int_{\Omega}\left(u-1-\ln u\right)\leq\frac{3}{4}\int_{\Omega}\left(u-1\right)^{2}, (4.41)

for all t>t0t>t_{0}, with C4>0C_{4}>0. This completes the proof. ∎

∫Ω(u−u¯−u¯​ln⁡uu¯)=∫Ω(ℋ⁡(u)−ℋ⁡(u¯))≤12​u¯​∫Ω(u−u¯)2,∀t>t0.\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}\left(u-\bar{u}-\bar{u}\ln\frac{u}{\bar{u}}\right)=\int_{\Omega}(\mathcal{H}(u)-\mathcal{H}(\bar{u}))\leq\frac{1}{2\bar{u}}\int_{\Omega}(u-\bar{u})^{2},\quad\forall\,t>t_{0}.

14​u^​∫Ω(u−u^)2≤∫Ω(u−u^−u^​ln⁡uu^)≤34​u^​∫Ω(u−u^)2,∀t>t0.\displaystyle\frac{1}{4\hat{u}}\int_{\Omega}(u-\hat{u})^{2}\leq\int_{\Omega}\left(u-\hat{u}-\hat{u}\ln\frac{u}{\hat{u}}\right)\leq\frac{3}{4\hat{u}}\int_{\Omega}(u-\hat{u})^{2},\quad\forall\,t>t_{0}. (4.49)

≤\displaystyle\leq −σ4κ8​ℰ4​(t),t>t0.\displaystyle-\frac{\sigma_{4}}{\kappa_{8}}\mathcal{E}_{4}(t),\qquad t>t_{0}.

5. Numerical examples

This section presents the results of numerical experiments conducted using the Finite Difference Method to investigate the behaviour of solutions to the predator-prey chemo-alarm-taxis system in both two- and three-dimensional spaces. We consider the initial-boundary value problem for the predator-prey chemo-alarm-taxis system (1), with radially symmetric bell-shaped initial condition

u(⋅,0)=e−0.1∑i=1nxi2,\displaystyle u(\cdot,0)=e^{-0.1\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}^{2}}, v(⋅,0)=3e−0.3∑i=1nxi2,\displaystyle v(\cdot,0)=3e^{-0.3\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}^{2}},
w(⋅,0)=2e−0.2∑i=1nxi2,\displaystyle w(\cdot,0)=2e^{-0.2\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}^{2}}, z(⋅,0)=e−0.1∑i=1nxi2.\displaystyle z(\cdot,0)=e^{-0.1\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}^{2}}.

In all of the examples presented below, we set di=1,i=1,2,3,4d_{i}=1,i=1,2,3,4, χ1=χ2=ξ=μ1=μ2=μ3=α=β=1\chi_{1}=\chi_{2}=\xi=\mu_{1}=\mu_{2}=\mu_{3}=\alpha=\beta=1, γ=2\gamma=2 and adopt a uniform grid Δxi=1101,i=1,2\Delta x_{i}=\frac{1}{101},i=1,2 for 2D and Δxi=150,i=1,2,3\Delta x_{i}=\frac{1}{50},i=1,2,3 for 3D within a domain [−0.5,0.5]n[-0.5,0.5]^{n}, where n=2,3n=2,3.

Let ai=0.5,i=1,2,3,4a_{i}=0.5,i=1,2,3,4, then the conditions given in (1) are satisfied. Therefore the solution (u,v,w,z)(u,v,w,z) converges to the coexistence steady state (ue,ve,we,ze)(u_{e},v_{e},w_{e},z_{e}) as t→∞t\to\infty.

Example 5.3 (Prey vanishing state).

Let a1=a3=0.01,a2=1,a4=3,a5=a6=2a_{1}=a_{3}=0.01,a_{2}=1,a_{4}=3,a_{5}=a_{6}=2, then conditions given in (1) are not satisfied and a3<1a_{3}<1. Therefore, the solution (u,v,w,z)(u,v,w,z) converges to the semi-coexistence (prey vanishing) steady state (u¯,v¯,w¯,z¯)(\bar{u},\bar{v},\bar{w},\bar{z}) as t→∞t\to\infty.

Remark 5.1.

When the conditions specified in Example 1 are sufficiently strong, the solution rapidly converges to the coexistence steady state. Conversely, when the conditions in Example 1 are not sufficiently strong, the solution quickly converges to the trivial steady state (1,0,0,0)(1,0,0,0).

6. Conclusion

We have investigated the global existence of a classical solution to system (1), which remains uniformly bounded in the ℒ∞​(Ω){\mathcal{L}^{\infty}}(\Omega) norm for dimensions n≥1n\geq 1, under suitable parameter conditions. Furthermore, we established global asymptotic stability by constructing an appropriate Lyapunov functional and verified these results through numerical simulations. Our analysis yielded several important stability outcomes with meaningful biological implications. In particular, the findings underscore the decisive role of the chemotaxis coefficients in governing the existence and stability of the predator–prey alarm-taxis system.
